fields.title: What the user sees: guarantees on their side
fields.keyTakeaway: A user needs not data freshness in general, but the visibility of their own actions and the absence of rollbacks — both are achieved cheaper than reading everything from the primary database.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: How to make sure a person does not notice lag without routing all reads to the primary database?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: The difference between a product that "behaves strangely sometimes" and a product people trust often lies precisely in this. A user forgives slowness. They do not forgive when their own action disappears — this looks like data loss, and after that they check everything manually.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: There are two guarantees that matter more to the user than formal data freshness.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[read-your-writes|Read your writes]].** A person must see their own change immediately. Other people's changes can lag — nobody will notice this because the person does not know when exactly they happened.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: Implemented simply: for some time after a write, this user's reads go to the primary. Or the change is displayed locally in the client without waiting for the server.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **[[monotonic-reads|Monotonic reads]].** Data must not roll back. If a person saw their review, and on the next refresh the review disappeared — this is worse than if the review had never appeared at all. Occurs when two consecutive requests hit different replicas with different lag. Fixed by pinning the user to a single replica within a session.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: The third technique is product-level, not technical: **honest intermediate state.** Not "review published" and not emptiness, but "review sent, will appear within a minute". A user calmly waits for what they were warned about and worries about what disappeared silently.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Order history is read from the replica, but for 30 seconds after checkout — from the primary. The threshold is chosen as the worst observed lag multiplied by three. The cost is fractions of a percent of load on the primary because the window is short.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Reviews were handled differently. Publication goes through moderation, meaning there is a delay anyway. Instead of a technical solution, a product one was written: the review immediately appears in the personal section with an "under review" badge and is visible to the author. Lag ceased to exist as a problem because the interface explained the delay that was already there.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: The reverse example we learned from: the counter "N items in cart" in the header was read from the replica. A person added an item, the counter did not change, the person added it again. Duplicates in the cart became a noticeable share of support tickets. Fixed by moving the counter to the client — it already knows what the person just clicked.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Guarantees on the user side do not replace strong consistency where it is fundamentally needed: money, stock, access rights. They solve the perception problem, not correctness.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A user needs not data freshness in general, but the visibility of their own actions and the absence of rollbacks — both are achieved cheaper than reading everything from the primary database.
